claim_comment: Closing recall semantics only after proving optional stable memory references, explicit policy-addressable provenance absence, non-comparable provider-native scores without host normalization, and exact temporal/scope behavior.
retry_note: The first evidence run rejected only a documentation phrase expressed as an inline field name. The documentation now states the canonical optional-stable-memory-reference rule explicitly; contract semantics and tests are unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: Missing provenance is explicit and policy-addressable.
Native score semantics cannot be compared across providers without normalization.
Temporal and scope semantics are unambiguous.
close_reason: Accepted the V1 provider-neutral recall contract with optional stable memory identity, explicit provenance policy, host-owned score normalization, exact coding scope, and deterministic temporal semantics.
close_comment: Evidence: provider-recall-contract.json and its strict schema define exact provider/registration/readiness/scope/request identity, current/as-of/interval/history semantics, finite handshake-clamped budgets, canonical exclusions, inert-or-explicit extensions, request-scoped candidate IDs, optional stable memory refs, exactly one content form, canonical content digests, typed references, provider-native score-domain metadata, TraceDecay-owned normalized scores, explicit validity/supersession/revocation, available/redacted/unavailable provenance with policy actions, bounded explanations, deterministic coverage/ordering, and typed recall states. Provider-native scores cannot be cross-compared without normalization; providers cannot supply normalized scores, widen scope, cross worktrees/branches/sessions, inject context, select the final pack, fabricate provenance, exceed budgets, ignore exclusions, or use empty candidates as failure/fallback. The validator cross-checks the accepted registry/handshake authorities and tests every acceptance criterion plus negative scope, temporal, score, provenance, extension, coverage, ordering, terminal, Beads, and schema cases.
